summary: Describes the CRONUS Virtual Local Network, especially its addressing features and a way to map between Internet addresses and local network addresses. It is meant to stimulate discussion rather than define a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to make a bunch of computers act like one tidy local network, with a method to translate between internet names and local ones.

questions: what is the cronus virtual local network
how does the vln map internet addresses to ethernet addresses
what addressing modes does the vln support
how does the vln guarantee datagram delivery
subtitle: A protocol layer that lets operating systems swap local networks transparently.

tldr.problem: The CRONUS Distributed Operating System needs to communicate over local networks while remaining compatible with the DARPA Internet protocols. Different clusters might use different physical networks, requiring a compatibility layer.
tldr.mechanism: The VLN sits between the IP layer and the physical network, providing a unified datagram interface that supports unicast, broadcast, and multicast addressing. It also defines a dynamic address mapping protocol for Ethernet implementations.
tldr.outcome: Applications can use standard IP over any physical local network via the VLN interface, and clusters can switch physical networks without rewriting software.

today: RFC 824 proposed an important design pattern: the protocol abstraction layer that hides network hardware differences while preserving compatibility with higher layers. While CRONUS itself did not become widely deployed, the principle of virtualizing the network interface influenced later system design. Virtual local networks remain relevant in modern infrastructure, and the dynamic address mapping approach anticipated techniques used in Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) and similar mechanisms.

sections.title: Purpose and the VLN Design Goals
sections.content:
The CRONUS Virtual Local Network (VLN) is an abstraction layer that provides host-to-host datagram communication for the CRONUS Distributed Operating System. It sits between the Internet Protocol and the physical local network, replacing direct access to the network hardware.

The VLN is designed with two main goals. Compatibility means the VLN transparently runs IP and TCP without modifications, so existing internet software can run on Cronus clusters unchanged. Substitutability means Cronus software depends only on the VLN interface, not on its implementation, so one physical network can be swapped for another by re-implementing just the VLN layer.

The VLN consists of a client interface specification and an implementation, which can vary based on the physical network hardware chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: The VLN is like a restaurant order window. Applications talk to it the same way every time, but behind the window it could send orders by bike, truck, or drone.

sections.title: VLN Addressing Modes
sections.content:
The VLN uses 32-bit internet addresses but assigns special meaning to the local address field. Unlike regular internet addresses, a single local address can refer to a specific host, all hosts in the cluster (broadcast), or groups of hosts (multicast).

Specific host addresses use values 0 to 1,023. Multicast addresses occupy 1,024 to 65,534, allowing groups of hosts to receive the same message. The broadcast address is 65,535, reaching every host in the cluster. A VLN network should be either class A or B to represent the full range of these address modes within the internet address structure.

This addressing scheme lets cluster hosts communicate with each other and with the broader internet using the same address space and internet protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The VLN reuses internet addresses but sneaks in three secret meanings: "one host", "a group", and "everybody." This lets it talk to the whole cluster without changing how IP works.

sections.title: VLN Operations and Reliability
sections.content:
Software accesses the VLN through seven operations: ResetVLNInterface clears the layer; MyVLNAddress returns the host's address; SendVLNDatagram transmits a datagram; ReceiveVLNDatagram waits for incoming datagrams; PurgeMAddresses unsubscribes from multicast; and AttendMAddress and IgnoreMAddress manage multicast group membership.

The VLN guarantees that datagrams of 576 octets or fewer can be delivered between any two hosts in the cluster. It also guarantees accuracy: received datagrams match transmitted ones because invalid frames are discarded. Datagrams do not duplicate during transmission. Within the same cluster, datagrams are received in order (though some may be lost).

Broadcast and multicast datagrams have a stronger sequencing guarantee: if multiple receivers get two broadcasts, they see them in the same order.
sections.plainLanguage: The VLN promises that messages sent to nearby neighbors arrive exactly as sent, don't get copied by accident, and stay in order. Large messages might get lost, but the ones that make it are reliable.

sections.title: Ethernet Implementation and Address Mapping
sections.content:
An Ethernet-based VLN faces a unique problem: Ethernet addresses are 48-bit quantities assigned by the manufacturer, not under the control of the network administrator. The VLN must dynamically map its 32-bit internet addresses to these physical addresses.

Each host establishes a virtual-to-physical map (VPMap) using a multicast mechanism. When a host boots, it creates a multicast address from its VLN address (the multicast host address, or MHA) and registers it with the Ethernet controller. When another host sends a message to an unmapped address, the frame goes to the MHA. The receiving host then broadcasts a mapping update containing its Ethernet address and VLN address. Other hosts update their VPMaps from this broadcast.

For multicast datagrams, the implementation adapts to different Ethernet controllers, which vary in their ability to recognize multicast addresses. The protocol uses Ethernet multicast when possible and falls back to broadcast for addresses beyond the controller's capability.
sections.plainLanguage: Ethernet addresses are random numbers the manufacturer printed on the card. The VLN asks "who are you?" by sending to a group address, and hosts answer "I'm address X, my Ethernet number is Y." Other hosts write this down so they know where to send next time.

sections.title: Compatibility with Internet Standards
sections.content:
The VLN places no requirements on IP; datagrams passed through the VLN interface have the same structure as standard IP datagrams. The VLN layer uses only the Source Address, Destination Address, Total Length, and Header Checksum fields from the IP header; other fields are passed through unchanged. It does not perform fragmentation, reassembly, or options processing-those remain IP's job.

This tight compatibility was intentional. By not extending IP, the design avoided lengthy delays in standards approval and allowed Cronus to assimilate existing internet software (email, remote terminal access, file transfer) into the system. The Cronus prototype (the Advanced Development Model) would connect to the ARPANET, and compatibility ensured it followed internet conventions.

The VLN shows how to abstract away network hardware while preserving full compatibility with layer 3 protocols, a principle useful beyond Cronus itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The VLN is sneaky: it looks exactly like the physical network to IP, so IP thinks it is talking to a regular LAN. This lets the Cronus team use existing internet software without changes.
